2027-06-25.title: Friday of the fifth week after Pentecost
readings: By faith Abraham offered up Isaac; by faith Isaac, Jacob and Joseph blessed the generations to come
“My teaching is not mine but his who sent me”; judge with right judgment
2027-06-25.alt: Season of Pentecost, the week after the Fifth Sunday after Pentecost, in the Apostles' Fast (Shleeha Nombu), which ends on 29 June. No commemoration is printed in the Panchangam today. A Friday of the fast.
2027-06-25.verse: Do not judge by appearances, but judge with right judgment.
theo: On this Friday of the Apostles' Fast, the Letter to the Hebrews takes us to the mountain where Abraham's faith was tried to the utmost: “By faith Abraham, when put to the test, offered up Isaac. He who had received the promises was ready to offer up his only son, of whom he had been told, ‘It is through Isaac that descendants shall be named for you.’” Everything God had promised seemed to hang on this one boy, and God asked for him. Abraham did not understand, but he trusted. The letter tells us what held him: “He considered the fact that God is able even to raise someone from the dead.” Abraham, whom Jews and Christians alike honour as our father in faith, believed that the God who gives life could give it back. The Fathers of the Church saw in Isaac, climbing the mountain with the wood on his shoulders, a figure of Christ carrying his cross; Origen told his hearers that Isaac bearing the wood for his own sacrifice shows us the Lord who carried the wood of the cross (Homilies on Genesis 8, in substance). On a Friday we remember that the Father did not withhold his only Son, and that the Son was truly raised from the dead.

The reading continues with three deathbeds and three blessings. “By faith Isaac invoked blessings for the future on Jacob and Esau. By faith Jacob, when dying, blessed each of the sons of Joseph, ‘bowing in worship over the top of his staff.’ By faith Joseph, at the end of his life, made mention of the exodus of the Israelites and gave instructions about his burial.” These old men could not see the fulfilment of the promise, but they handed it on. Faith looks forward; it blesses those who will live after us. In our homes the elders still make the sign of the cross on the foreheads of children before a journey, an examination or the first day of school. This month, as the schools reopen, that small gesture is repeated in thousands of houses. It is not a superstition; it is the faith of Isaac and Jacob, a blessing given by those who believe that God will keep his promises to the next generation even when they are no longer here to see it.

In the Gospel Jesus teaches in the temple at the feast of Tabernacles, and his hearers are astonished: “How does this man have such learning, when he has never been taught?” Jesus does not boast of his learning. He points away from himself: “My teaching is not mine but his who sent me. Anyone who resolves to do the will of God will know whether the teaching is from God or whether I am speaking on my own.” Here is a key to the life of faith: understanding comes to those who obey. St Augustine, commenting on these words, told his people that if they did not yet understand, they should believe and do the will of God, for understanding is the reward of faith (Tractates on John 29, in substance). When the evangelist writes “the Jews” here, he means the religious authorities in Jerusalem who opposed Jesus, not a whole people; the Church teaches that the Jewish people as such may not be blamed for the death of Christ (Catechism 597). Jesus then defends his healing of a man on the sabbath and ends with a word for every age: “Do not judge by appearances, but judge with right judgment.” The fast is a time to cleanse our judgements too: to stop judging others by their clothes, their caste, their accent or their past, and to look, as God does, at the heart.
outline: Ask: what blessing have I received from those before me, and what blessing will I hand on?
Abraham on the mountain: trust in the God who can raise the dead.
Isaac, Jacob and Joseph hand on the promise; the sign of the cross on a child's forehead.
The teaching that comes from the Father, understood by those who do his will; not judging by appearances.
“Do not judge by appearances, but judge with right judgment.”
live: Make the sign of the cross on the forehead of a child, a grandchild or a godchild this week, and pray for them by name.
Catch yourself the next time you judge someone by appearance, and say a prayer for that person instead.
2027-06-25.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, on this Friday we remember that the Father did not withhold you, his only Son, but gave you up for us all, and raised you from the dead. Give us the faith of Abraham, who trusted when he did not understand, and the faith of Isaac, Jacob and Joseph, who blessed the generations to come. Teach us to do the will of the Father, so that we may know that your teaching is from God. Cleanse our hearts of rash and proud judgements, and let us look on others as you look on them. You live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: Abraham went up the mountain trusting that God would provide; at the Holy Qurbono the Lamb whom God provided is offered, and the sacrifice of Calvary is made present for us on the altar.

quick: By faith Abraham was ready to offer Isaac, trusting that God could even raise the dead.
By faith Isaac, Jacob and Joseph blessed the generations to come, though they did not see the promise fulfilled.
Jesus says his teaching comes from the Father; whoever does God's will shall know it. Do not judge by appearances.
2027-06-25.action: Bless a child or a younger person today with the sign of the cross, and pray for their future.
2027-06-25.question: Do I judge people by appearances, or do I try to see them as God sees them?

family.explain: Long ago, when Isaac and Jacob were very old, they blessed their children and grandchildren and asked God to take care of them. In our family too, grandparents and parents bless children with the sign of the cross. Jesus also tells us not to judge people by how they look, but to look at their hearts, as God does.
family.intention: We pray for all the grandparents and parents in our family, and for the children who receive their blessing.
family.ask: Ask: “Is there someone at school or at work whom I have judged by how they look? How can I get to know them better?”

illus: A mother in Idukki has blessed her children every morning since they were small: before they leave the house, she makes the sign of the cross on their foreheads with her thumb and whispers a short prayer. Her eldest son is now a policeman and wears a uniform and a cap, and she still does it at the door, standing on tiptoe. Once a colleague who had come to pick him up laughed and asked whether he still needed his mother's permission to go to work. The son answered quietly: it is not permission, it is a blessing, and in my job I have learned to want every blessing I can get. Some weeks later the same colleague asked her, a little shyly, whether she would bless him too.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, give us the faith of Abraham and the faith of our fathers and mothers. Teach us to bless those who come after us, and to judge with right judgment. Amen.
share: By faith Abraham, when put to the test, offered up Isaac (Hebrews 11:17). What test has God allowed in my life, and how have I answered?
By faith Isaac invoked blessings for the future on Jacob and Esau (Hebrews 11:20). Who blessed me, and whom do I bless?
Do not judge by appearances, but judge with right judgment (John 7:24). Whom have I judged unfairly?
interc: For the Church, that she may hand on the faith of the Apostles faithfully to the next generation.
For grandparents and parents, that they may bless their children and teach them by their example.
For children and students at the start of the school year, that they may grow in wisdom and in grace.
For all who are judged unfairly because of their appearance, their caste, their poverty or their past, that they may find justice and respect.
For all who keep the Apostles' Fast, that their hearts may be purified and their judgements made right.
pm.close: Father, you tested the faith of Abraham and gave him back his son. Strengthen our faith in times of trial, make us a blessing to those who come after us, and teach us to see others with your eyes. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear friends, today the Letter to the Hebrews tells us: By faith Abraham, when put to the test, offered up Isaac (Hebrews 11:17). It was the hardest test of his life. Isaac was the son of the promise. But Abraham trusted, because he considered the fact that God is able even to raise someone from the dead (Hebrews 11:19). On this Friday we think of the Father who gave his own Son for us, and raised him from the dead.

Then the letter speaks of old men blessing their children: by faith Isaac invoked blessings for the future on Jacob and Esau (Hebrews 11:20), and Jacob, when dying, blessed each of the sons of Joseph (Hebrews 11:21). They did not see the promise fulfilled, but they passed it on. Our elders still bless children with the sign of the cross before school and before journeys. That is the faith of the patriarchs living in our homes.

In the Gospel, people are amazed at the teaching of Jesus. He says: My teaching is not mine but his who sent me. Anyone who resolves to do the will of God will know whether the teaching is from God (John 7:16–17). If we want to understand our faith, we must begin by living it. Then Jesus adds: Do not judge by appearances, but judge with right judgment (John 7:24).

So on this Friday of the fast, let us ask for a faith that trusts in hard times, a faith that blesses the next generation, and a heart that does not judge by appearances. Let us bless our children, and let us look at every person as God looks at them. Amen.
kids: Children, does your grandmother or your mother make a little cross on your forehead before you go to school? That is a blessing! Long ago, Isaac and Jacob, who were very old, also blessed their children and grandchildren and asked God to take care of them. And Jesus tells us something important: do not judge people by how they look. A new boy or girl in your class may look different, but God loves them very much. Be kind to them!

intro: Theme: “Do not judge by appearances, but judge with right judgment.”

On Friday of the fifth week after Pentecost, in the Apostles' Fast: Abraham's offering, the patriarchs who blessed the generations to come, and the teaching of Jesus understood by those who do God's will.

sub: The God who can raise the dead.
Isaac with the wood, a figure of Christ with the cross.
q: Abraham said, “God himself will provide the lamb for a burnt offering, my son.”
He who did not withhold his own Son, but gave him up for all of us, will he not with him also give us everything else?
points.apply: Hand over to God in prayer one thing you are afraid to lose.

sub: Isaac, Jacob and Joseph at the end of life.
They did not see the promise but handed it on.
The sign of the cross on a child's forehead.
q: we will tell to the coming generation the glorious deeds of the Lord, and his might, and the wonders that he has done.
I am reminded of your sincere faith, a faith that lived first in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice and now, I am sure, lives in you.
points.apply: Bless the children of your home each morning this week before they leave.

sub: A teaching that comes from the Father.
Understanding is the reward of faith.
Not by appearances but by the heart.
q: for the Lord does not see as mortals see; they look on the outward appearance, but the Lord looks on the heart.
Do not judge, so that you may not be judged.
points.apply: Speak a kind word this week to someone you have judged by appearances.

concl: Faith trusts in the God who raises the dead, and blesses those who will come after us.
The one who does God's will comes to know the truth, and learns to see others as God sees them.
2027-06-25.resolve: Trust like Abraham, bless like Isaac and Jacob, and judge with right judgment.
